name: Common method bias
statement: Common method bias is the claim that two constructs measured by the same instrument, usually one self-report survey, correlate partly because of the shared method.
meaning: This is a property of a research design rather than a habit of a mind, which it shares with selection bias and survivorship bias and with little else in this collection. A respondent who answers questions about job satisfaction and about supervisor behaviour in one sitting brings something to both answers that belongs to neither construct: an acquiescent style, a wish to look consistent, a mood, the position of the items on the page. Podsakoff, MacKenzie, Lee and Podsakoff define common method variance as "variance that is attributable to the measurement method rather than to the constructs the measures represent". Doty and Glick separate two things the literature runs together. Common method variance is how much of the variance in a measure the method accounts for. Common method bias is "the divergence between observed and true relationships among constructs", which is the quantity a reader of a results table actually cares about. The two are not the same number and can move in opposite directions. Citing Cote and Buckley's 1988 work, Podsakoff and colleagues note that method effects inflate an observed relationship when the correlation between the methods is higher than the correlation between the measures with method effects removed, and deflate it when the correlation between the methods is lower. The response styles that supply much of this variance are the subject of the response bias entry, which is not repeated here.

origin.who: Philip M. Podsakoff, Scott B. MacKenzie, Jeong-Yeon Lee and Nathan P. Podsakoff
origin.note: "Common Method Biases in Behavioral Research: A Critical Review of the Literature and Recommended Remedies", 88(5), 879 to 903. The paper did not coin the idea and says so, opening with the observation that "discussions of the potential impact of common method biases date back well over 40 years" and citing Campbell and Fiske's 1959 multitrait-multimethod matrix. What 2003 established was the checklist form in which reviewers now apply the concern. The numbers it rests on are older, from Cote and Buckley's 1987 meta-analysis of 70 construct-validation datasets.

evidence: The quantitative base is a small set of meta-analyses that refit confirmatory factor models to previously published multitrait-multimethod matrices. Cote and Buckley examined 70 published datasets and report in their abstract that "on average, traits account for less than 50% of the variance in construct measures". The figure everyone quotes from that paper, 26.3% of the variance in a typical research measure, is read here from Podsakoff and colleagues' 2003 account, which calls it variance "due to systematic sources of measurement error like common method biases" rather than to method alone. The same account records that the share varied by field, lowest in marketing at 15.8% and highest in education at 30.5%, and by construct, 22.5% for typical job performance measures against 40.7% for attitude measures. Podsakoff, MacKenzie and Podsakoff summarise five such meta-analyses in their 2012 review and conclude that "18% to 32% of the total variance in the items used in these studies was due to method factors". Doty and Glick assessed every multitrait-multimethod matrix published over 12 years in six social science journals and report that 46% of the variation in measures is attributable to the constructs, 32% to common method variance, and that this "results in a 26% bias in the observed relationships among constructs". Their own verdict on that figure is that it "is cause for concern but does not invalidate many research findings". The largest single number in the literature comes from comparing sources rather than decomposing variance. Podsakoff and colleagues pooled meta-analyses that had tested rating source as a moderator and found the average corrected correlation between leader behaviours and outcomes was 0.456 from the same source and 0.191 from different sources. Their Table 2 defines its inflation percentage as the ratio of the two corrected correlations and gives 239% for that pairing, with six others at 212%, 148%, 208%, 133%, 304% and 184%. The running text of the same review gives 213% and 147% for the second and third of those, so the table and the prose disagree on two figures. The authors add that some of the gap may be raters seeing different things rather than method bias. Item placement has been manipulated directly. Weijters, Geuens and Schillewaert modelled the correlation between all pairs of 76 items on data from 2,850 respondents, and as their result is reported in the 2012 review, two items measuring unrelated constructs correlated 0.04 when six items apart and 0.09 when adjacent. The conditions are common. That review reports Bodner's finding that 76% of studies across six areas of psychology used a single measurement method. A 2025 study made the point without a matrix. Joel, Sakaluk, Kim, Khera, Qin and Stanton wrote ten relationship items with the key noun replaced by a plant or a mineral, such as "My partner and I have excellent taro", and called the scale Pseudo. In a pilot of 331 people one factor accounted for 58% of the variance and all ten items loaded above .70. Among 477 people in long-term relationships, recruited as 495 and reduced by 18 who did not qualify, Pseudo correlated .43 to .58 with satisfaction, commitment, appreciation and trust, against .60 to .80 among those four measures themselves.

replication.headline: The measurement has been repeated and agrees; the interpretation has been repeated and does not, with estimates of how much the bias distorts a correlation running from 18% of item variance to a 92% inflation of observed relationships.
replication.detail: There is no single experiment here to re-run, so the closest available thing is re-analysis of the same multitrait-multimethod archive by different teams. On the size of the method component they converge. The 2012 review's Table 1 gives Cote and Buckley 26% method variance across 70 matrices, Williams, Cote and Buckley 25% across 11, Buckley and colleagues 22% across 61, Doty and Glick 32% across 28, and Lance and colleagues 18% across 18, a span of 18% to 32%. On what that does to a research finding they split. Lance, Dawson, Birkelbach and Hoffman put method variance at 18%, lower than earlier reviews, and report that although common method variance does inflate observed relationships, "this effect is almost completely offset by the attenuating effect of measurement error". Doty and Glick, from the same kind of data, get a 26% bias they call cause for concern. Podsakoff and colleagues, applying their own decomposition to Cote and Buckley's figures, calculate inflation of about 45%, and list 38% from Buckley and colleagues, 92% from Doty and Glick and 60% from Lance and colleagues. They concede the estimates overlap and are not independent, and that the spread runs from 38% to 92%. They also note that a single-method design implies a method correlation of 1.00, on which the same estimates would run from 94% to 270%. Crampton and Wagner tested the pattern across the published record instead, analysing 42,934 correlations in 581 articles. They found general evidence of percept-percept inflation, and on a subsample of 11,710 correlations concluded it "has not had the broad, comprehensive effects envisioned by critics", so that "domain-specific investigations are required".

study.cite: Lance, C. E., Dawson, B., Birkelbach, D., & Hoffman, B. J. (2010). Method Effects, Measurement Error, and Substantive Conclusions. Organizational Research Methods, 13(3), 435-455.

limits: No replication in the ordinary sense is available. Searches of Crossref, PubMed and the open web on 21 September 2026 for a registered report or a multi-site repetition of a common method bias finding returned re-analyses of shared archives, simulations and new demonstrations rather than repetitions; OpenAlex answered single records but rate-limited the search queries that day. Two recent studies are empirical rather than archival. Joel and colleagues preregistered the dyadic half of their Pseudo work, and Rubenstein, Simon, Kammeyer-Mueller, Corwin, Morrison and Whiting report "an initial study and a constructive replication" in which a psychological separation task of at least 7.5 minutes attenuated correlations about as much as temporal separation or distinct sources did. Their full text was not obtained and only the PubMed abstract informs this entry. The sceptical case is that the standard framing gets the mechanism wrong. Spector's paper argues that the popular position "suggesting CMV automatically affects variables measured with the same method is a distortion and oversimplification of the true state of affairs, reaching the status of urban legend", and proposes retiring the term in favour of "measurement bias that is the product of the interplay of constructs and methods by which they are assessed". His 1987 study of affective and perceptual work measures found "little evidence for method variance as a biasing problem" and concluded that properly developed instruments of that type resist it, while adding that their validity cannot be assumed from that result. Only the abstracts of both papers were obtained, the 2006 one at the University of South Florida repository, which carries no file, and the 1987 one at OpenAlex. Spector, Rosen, Richardson, Williams and Johnson later set out the positive version of the argument, that shared sources of method variance inflate a correlation while unshared sources attenuate it. The remedies are weaker than the diagnosis. Richardson, Simmering and Sturman ran 691,200 simulated datasets against three post hoc corrections and doing nothing. Where no common method variance existed, correction in most conditions produced less accurate estimates than no correction, and all three techniques falsely identified bias about half the time when the true correlation was above zero. The exceptions matter: with an ideal marker the correlational marker beat no correction at a true correlation of zero, and the confirmatory factor analysis marker beat it above zero. Across all conditions the unmeasured latent method construct approach identified the presence or absence of common method variance correctly about 41% of the time, the correlational marker approach about 69%, and the confirmatory factor analysis marker 73%, rising to about 84% with ideal markers only. Their summary is that they "cannot recommend any post hoc CMV technique as a means for correcting CMV's potential effects", though they do suggest the confirmatory factor analysis marker as a way to test for its presence. Fuller, Simmering, Atinc, Atinc and Babin note that many business researchers test for the problem and "almost no one reports problematic findings", and their simulation concludes that at typical reliabilities and effect sizes common method variance "does not represent a grave threat to the validity of research findings". Podsakoff, Podsakoff, Williams, Huang and Yang answered in 2024 with a review titled "Common Method Bias: It's Bad, It's Complex, It's Widespread, and It's Not Easy to Fix". Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar both record it as hybrid open access under a CC BY licence at the publisher, and on 21 September 2026 the publisher's article page, its PDF, the Ingenta mirror and the SSRN copy all returned HTTP 403 pages carrying a Cloudflare managed bot challenge rather than a subscription notice. The article is open and was still not obtained, so only its Crossref abstract informs this entry and none of its figures are quoted here.
misreadings: The first error is treating a same-source design as proof that a result is inflated. Direction is not fixed. Podsakoff and colleagues' 2003 paper states that the evidence from Cote and Buckley's 70 studies "indicates that the observed relationship between a typical predictor and criterion variable is understated by approximately 26% because of common method biases", while their 2012 review calculates about 45% inflation from the same estimates. Both wordings are on the page in the two papers, and a reader who has met only the phrase "inflated correlation" will find the pair surprising. Response styles cut the same two ways. In Baumgartner and Steenkamp's data, as the 2012 review reports it, a true positive correlation paired with negatively correlated response style components fell by 55%. The second error is reading Harman's single-factor test as a control. Podsakoff and colleagues are blunt that the procedure "actually does nothing to statistically control for (or partial out) method effects", that it is at best an insensitive diagnostic, and that finding more than one factor "is not evidence that the measures are free of common method variance". They do not recommend it, and it remains the most reported remedy. The third error is dismissing a moderation result as method artefact. Siemsen, Roth and Oliveira show that common method variance can inflate or deflate a bivariate linear relationship depending on how symmetrically it hits the measures, and that "quadratic and interaction effects cannot be artifacts of CMV", though both can be severely deflated by it. An interaction found in single-source data is the one result the objection cannot touch. The fourth error is reading Spector as denying that method affects measurement. His argument is about sufficiency, that the method alone does not produce the bias and that constructs and methods interact, which is why his proposed replacement is more design work rather than less. The fifth is reading Joel and colleagues' nonsense scale as a clean win. Pseudo predicted later satisfaction, commitment, appreciation and trust when the week 1 measure was controlled, but with the week 2 measure controlled it predicted satisfaction at p = .176 and commitment at p = .060.
